speaker: Speaker 1
words: The following interview of Elsie Nelson was taped by Isabel Miller early in the year 1975 in Moscow, Idaho.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's all it has to be. It's kind of nice to grow old and have as many friends as I have. I just feel happy. And I just, even if I get so busy, I don't have time to eat, I certainly have three syrups so that I don't mind that. But, you know, I feel that...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Excuse me, I'm going to get my hat so that'll be...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Would you like to have a table? I've got cardigans right there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, this is fine. I just want that the microphone works better if it's on a thing like that so there won't be any vibration. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, when I try to... You know, once in a while when I sit here at night, well then I get an inspiration or I think of something that I want to put down because I... So I say when you get to be four years old, why you don't know how many more years you're going to be here. And when I see some of the pitiful things, I say, well people have been here lately, they were real bright in their mind before just a year or two ago, you know. One of them, Miss Spag's husband. The other day, Mrs. Mr. Maranoff came up and he just felt terrible.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, that's an important thing for you to be doing now, isn't it? To record things and to get... And to now get...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Now, like, one thing I want to do... You don't have that on because I wanted to ask you a few questions there that we don't have to be in here. And my little grandnephew and his sister and brother went there. And my brother, Carl, from California, who has a beautiful home and everything in California. All of them are scattered throughout the states, the different states, you know. And he said, oh, he said, this house, he said, you know what I used to do when I was a kid? I used to be an armory, he said, and I used to do all kinds of things. And those kids perked up their ears and that was fun. And we went into the bathroom and they had to take the bathtub out because the floor had rotted. So they took the bathtub and the old-fashioned bathtub. And that's a story by itself that when we got the bathtub, you know, that's described in the book. I told that story. And he said, see this plaster here? It looks like it's been passed, he said. Right under, it used to be the roller towel, the roller for the towel was above it, see. And we used to have roller towels, linen crèche, made out of linen crèche that Mother made, you know. She'd buy a whole bowl of linen crèche and make these roller towels because they were easy to wash. They were linen crèche. And he said one time they didn't let me go with them to town. They had the horse and buggy and I helped them hitch up the horse and buggy. And my goodness, they didn't let me go to town. I just had to stay home and I was mad, he said. And so when I got in here to wash my hands in the bathtub, I just thought I'm just going to knock that wall off. And I took my fist and he showed them how he took his fist and just put his fist through that wall right below the towel rack. And cracked the plaster, made a hole in it so they had to pass that. And the little man, grandnephew, Stevie, said, did you, Uncle Carl, did you really do that? He said, I sure did. And that just thrilled him. Well, and then we were in the old dining room. That old dining room reminded us both of how Mother used to always have a Christmas cactus there. And in the winter we walked home from school. And, well, we walked most all the time. But in the wintertime, sometimes Dad would take the sleigh and go and get her. Well, we didn't have any telephones. Not until 1916. So he'd just hook up the bob sled and a team of horses and go to a certain place where he used to stop. And if it was a real bad day, well, we knew he'd be there to take us home. And so, well, we did one or two of the kids that got there first and watched for him and then signaled to the others. So we all had to go at the same time, you know. We all got out of school. We were all out of school. Well, I doubt if I was in that. I imagine maybe I was in high school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you come into Moscow?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Sure. We went to Moscow all the time. And I went to – I'm the only one that went to country school. And I went there for three weeks, only three weeks, because they found out that we had to walk over to that country school over by Tomas Butte.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was east of your house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, quite east. And we walked there. But we didn't belong to this. But our farm and our house was in the school district, the Moscow school district. So we had to go there. So from then on, we were real happy. I've told that, too. And, well, we – so we walked around and this window, I was going to tell you, Mother always had her cactus, and it always bloomed before Christmas. It's great. We had that – it was 50 years old when I just had to – I went to Europe and I just didn't take care of it. And I was supposed to take care of it at the hotel. Well, I asked somebody else to take care of it, and they did. But it just was solid with blooms. And Mother, she just loved flowers, and she knew how to take care of them. And we always had nice flowers and plants in the house. And so this was another time that he had to stay home, see. And he broke – he did that accidentally, though. I don't remember. He knocked something in the window on the outside and broke that dining room window. So Dad, my father, always repaired the window panes when they broke. You know, they'd take putty – you know what that is? Yes, I do.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Putty and stuff. Stuff that around the edges. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And he just always – and he took – got the pane in town, and when he got home, it was broken. Most likely it got broken in this ladder wagon. And so he couldn't put it in then. We still had to have a rag or something in our window. Cold, too. And then he went a second time, and he had bad luck with it this time, and it broke again. When the pane was broken, when he got home, he thought he was careful. But I'm not sure that he took it home. I think the hired men took it home. We used to always have a hired man when the boys were small, see. And he was paid by the year and lived and ate there at the house. He was paid by the year. Well, so Dad says, I know what I'm going to do. I'm going to walk to town. That's two miles, a little over two miles. And I bet I'll come home with it. And he did. He walked to town, and he brought the pane home and put it there. Now, when we look back and think what effort they had to go through, there was nobody to call. You just had to take care of your problems.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, farmers had to be self-sufficient.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They had to be self-sufficient. And luckily, my father was aggressive, and he didn't believe in painting the house or papering the walls and things like that, like some farmers try to do everything. He said, well, my job is to farm now and get good grouts. And I'll hire somebody to. Like we papered maybe the dining room and the kitchen for Christmas and had everything ready for our big Christmas day. If you're going to have a history, I'm going to give you a description of Christmas at home.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, I'd like to hear that. But be sure you tell us now what your mother did all the time. Yeah. Especially we're interested in what the women were doing in those days.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I'll just be sure and tell you. I'll finish telling this about my brother. And then fix that. Well, then, so we got to, but we always have, I won't tell the Christmas story yet. Okay. All right. And we were going to school and walking to school. And one thing, when we got to the crossing, we walked on the railroad track. And we walked on this because it wasn't muddy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right. You walked on a tide.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and it was closer. And so we just skipped along the tides, you know. And we had to walk three-quarters of a mile till we got to that corner. And then we went on the tide clear down to almost town. Then we took off, and there was supposed to be sidewalks, but there wasn't. And in the summertime, our shoes got pretty dusty. And like on Sunday school and that, well, we'd stop at my grandma's house. That's my maternal grandmother's grandfather's. They always had a nice place, and they lived in this part. In fact, they didn't live very far from here. And so we'd always plan to cut across and go by their house and say hi to grandma and grandpa, you know. And then they'd always, grandpa would always go and get a rag, you know, wipe off your shoes before you go to school. And that was Sunday and Monday, you might say, all the time. And we'd stop, you know, just a few minutes because we wouldn't have much time. And so then we had to take our lunches to school. We brought our lunches, old hot lunches. And we always had good clothes, not jeans.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was important for your family, wasn't it? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And well, that picture there of the brothers, you saw that picture. There were seven brothers. Three of them were older, then one sister, and then four of them were younger. And then my younger sister. And I was the oldest. And so we brought our lunches. And I guess that's all right to tell that now. Oh, yeah. And I got up early in the morning when I got up after I was, about the time that we were all going to school. Maybe not all of us. Maybe there were two at home that were small, too small to go to school. But there were at least six. There were ten of us altogether. And there were at least six, the five brothers, at least five brothers, and myself and my sister that had lunch. We, my mother always baked bread. She'd make 40 loaves of bread a week when we were all, and 22 times a week she made all the bread. And she'd bake all, she made rolls and ruts. She made buns, good buns, and made them into ruts. And they were good. We'd put a little butter on them and eat them with our milk, coffee. We got a little bit of coffee in our milk sometimes. Just begged for it. And Mother let us have it. Didn't hurt us either. And we all had good meals, and she always, and I fixed the lunches in the morning. First I got the breakfast started. I got up at five o'clock. I've done it most of my life, most of my life. And then I'd start the breakfast. That is, I'd build a fire in the kitchen stove, see, and put the coffee on and maybe the water for the mush. And then Mother would help see that the children were getting dressed, you know, the younger children. By this time, several of them were able to dress themselves, see. And then when I got my breakfast started, Mother'd get down, and I put up all these lunches. And I made sandwiches, and we all had home cured meat. And that she'd even have cooked, or else we had dried beef, chipped beef, you know, that was cured and cured, you know. And, you know, a dried beef was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you make the dried beef there? Yeah, we made it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My father, they butchered before Christmas, and then they butchered several times. But when they butchered before Christmas, about two or three weeks before Christmas, why, they would take, eat as much of the meat as fresh as possible, like roast and that, because it was usually cold. We didn't have any cold storage or even refrigeration, but we had a cellar that was cold. And, but it just wouldn't keep very long, you know, that way. So we had it cured. And then we'd have chickens and roast goose and roast duck and all those things, and even some wild meat sometimes. But we used that for our sandwiches, and then we'd always have cupcakes or cookies or something sweet, you know, and always apples, good apples. We had a whole big orchard of wonderful apple trees. And so we always had apples. Well, the boys didn't want to have a lunchbox. Oh, not Elsie either. So they, I wrapped the sandwiches in paraffin paper, and Mother bought this paraffin paper nearest I can remember. She bought it in rolls, some kind of wax paper. It wasn't paraffin paper like we have now. But it was not anything like that. It was some kind of, it was heavier, kind of wax paper. And I just was very stingy with that, because we were stingy about what we used. We didn't waste anything. And then we'd wrap the sandwich in that, and then wrap newspapers around it. We had enough newspapers. Some farmers didn't have that many newspapers. Maybe they'd have one a week. But we always had enough newspapers or paper. And then we always saved our wrapping sacks and paper that we got our groceries. But we wouldn't put them in a big sack, you know, our lunch. We didn't want that. We wanted a small one. And then we'd put string around them. We'd save our string from our groceries and our packages. And Mother'd wind it around a ball, you know, or make a ball out of it and have it. And I had plenty of string for the, you know. And then the kids would put them in their coat pocket or just carry them like that on their fingers and eat them. And then they could throw that away. They didn't have to bother about blood sparks. And I didn't have to wash them, so I was glad of that. Because I just hated that. Yes. And then we always had dinner when we got home. Mother'd plan it so that when all of us were home, and we all got home about the same time, because even when we walked, the young ones could walk home alone. But if I was in high school, maybe I'd walk home alone, too, when it was nice. And when it was bad, I had to arrange to get there on that transportation, whatever my father had, the old hack or else the sleigh. And then the younger children had to wait someplace, wait in school. They let them do that. They had to let them do it. And then Mother had a dinner. And she always had a good dinner. We used to have fresh meat lots of times, because we'd buy fresh meat. When we didn't have any other fresh meat, we'd have fresh meat part of the time. But we also had roast pork and beef, because they'd kill a beef. The neighbors would get together, and they'd kill one young beef, or maybe we'd have veal roast or something like. We'd take a half of the beef, and the neighbors would take a half or something like that, or maybe even two or three farmers. And they divided it up that way so they could have fresh meat. Pork chops. Then we had chicken. We had turkey. We had beef. And so we always had a good dinner and always had dessert. My mother made wonderful pie. She made her pie out of lard mostly. But she made real good crust.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That would have come from the hogs that you butchered.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, that's right. We scarcely ever bought any of the short meat. And for cookies and cake and that, we always had plenty of butter. And we used that for short meat. We even fried chickens in butter a lot of times, because we had plenty of butter. And Mother didn't sell all the butter. Some farmers, they sold us all, and they just didn't have much. But I think our family was, on the average, just as well taken care of as anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But your mother thought good food was important.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My mother was very conservative. And she had been raised an only child, you might say. She was 14 years old when her one brother was born. So she was almost out of the way and married before he was very large. So she'd been raised in town. She'd never been on a farm before. And it was a new experience to her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you think it was hard for her to get adjusted?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I wouldn't say that, because I can't maybe, I don't remember the first year. But I just don't believe so, because she was really, I say, I've told my homemade friends, and I have a lot of homemade friends. And I wasn't especially interested in homemade cooking. My mother did most of the cooking. I took care of the kids' clothes and the house. I loved to keep house. And I'd clean the house and that. The boys were supposed to help me, like taking care of the rugs and that, upstairs, carry them down and that. But by the time that I got started and had my beds all fixed up and that, we had six beds. And I'm talking about a certain period when most of us were growing up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, the busiest time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And then there were still some babies. And my sister, as I said, was born 20 years after I was, the youngest.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So the boys were to help you in the house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They were supposed to help me. They did a lot, too. But then when I was going to clean, I'd maybe carry the rugs down, get them shipped, hang them out on the line. My grandmother wove rugs for us. My mother would get the yarn, or the carpet rag, we'd call them, and roll them in the ball.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Old clothes that you'd outgrown and worn out.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and lots of times the best ones were clothes that harvested some of the men that worked there. We always had men working there because the brothers weren't old enough yet. And they were starting, maybe one or two of them. Like this brother, Carl, he wasn't more than eight or nine years old. He could milk cows like a man.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They started early in those days. Yeah, they did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And they liked the milking. Now there'd be two of the brothers that kind of be given that chore to do. And then when they grew up so they could do other things, well, then the next two and the next two. And they worked in relays like that. In other words, my mother was a very good organizer, and my father followed suit because my father was a very kind man. And my mother was unequaled when it came to organizing her family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How do you remember that they made decisions? Did they talk things over? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they did. And what my mother, if my mother disciplined the boys in any way or any of us, why she, or my father did, why my mother never go over his, contradict his wishes, you know. She'd go along with him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Whatever he said.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There wasn't even a discussion because that was just a natural thing in our family. And she did most of the discipline because my father just didn't even like to do that. I don't remember, and most of the brothers don't remember ever getting spanked by Dad.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, he didn't question anything she did, he did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no, that's right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So it was mutual respect.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was just taken for granted. That's the way it was supposed to be. And, of course, Mother had to, bought the food and the work. And, oh, we just did an awful lot of work, you know. Like in the summertime, we canned 350 half-gallon jars, half-gallon jars of fruit and vegetables that was raised on the farm. And I'll pick cherries. The boys were supposed to help me pick cherries, but I think I did more than my share. And I could climb those cherry trees just as good as the boys. And I stayed with it and they didn't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you had a little more to fix the cherries.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because they had to go out and help Dad, you know, or something like that. They always found a good excuse.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right, they served Dad a lot with boys.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and then another thing in the summertime, why, no, I'm just really not very consistent, I suppose, but in the summertime, why, it was easier to raise boys on the farm than girls, you know. And they had their overalls, like we called them, and they had to wear shoes and stockings, because my dad would not let them go barefoot. He said, I'd rather pay for shoes and stockings than Dr. Bill.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, what would you wear in the summertime when you were climbing trees and things?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I never had any special shoes that I can remember.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But did you wear overalls, too?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, no, oh, no. I wore dresses.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You always had to wear dresses.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I always wore dresses. I had maybe one or two good dresses, and that was it. And I usually got one for Christmas that Mother had a dressmaker make, and she would get a dressmaker come out the house and sew for her and sew for me. Because there wasn't any ready-made clothes. You couldn't buy ready-made clothes for even the children like you can now, except that they bought shoes for the boys, and they bought shoes. And Mother insisted on having, and she knew, good material. And she insisted on having good material, and if the clerks didn't have it, she'd go to the big department. The only one that was here was really David, and then there was a mother wheeler, a G.C. Williamson's. Maybe you've heard of Williamson's. That was in the brown block, you know, or the Petuna. And they were those two. But if she couldn't get clothes for the children there, the ready-made clothes for the boys, and even the smaller children, she'd buy the boys, she'd buy. . . Went to town and bought him a real beautiful brown, breast to brown, they called it, if you had kind of a long coat like, and then little puffy short pants, puffy pants. And it was so cute, but that was the very latest, and they bought that for him. That was when he was little. There was, maybe all the children were born by that time, but he got that. And then the older boys, maybe two of them, were wearing long pants, they called them, and a suit, and mother would buy a suit for each one every year, and it had to be a real good material, a lot of blue serge, that's what they wore a lot.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they bought them new every year, so there wasn't any hand-me-downs then in your family.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, not, well, yes. Some. But they bought a new suit for all the boys every year, with two pairs of pants, see, they wore them to school. And the first year they wore them to church, you know, Sunday school, and for good. They had to have a good suit, so that if they were, well, if they were going to take them to someplace else besides church, why, they took the kids to circus, and they took them to different entertainments, and the older ones got to go to the show, they had to walk in. My brother, Whitey, that stayed with me, he told about going to that first silent picture, and it was right down there where that door is.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Fabric shop.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was the first show, and I couldn't even remember that, but he said that, and he said that we paid five cents a piece to go in there. And he was maybe 13 or 14, and Carl was older. Maybe he was 10 or 11 when he got to go the first time, and Carl and my older brother were older.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you get a new dress every, you said for Christmas?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I got a real nice dress for Christmas always, mothered by the prettiest material, and it was nearly always wool, or wool and silk.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did she pick it out?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes, I say so. And she picked it out, and she picked out the patterns. She had pretty good taste, but I wouldn't say this dressmaker did. She was a little bit old-fashioned. And I didn't. And there was another dressmaker, and sometimes she couldn't get it done, and I was always happy when she couldn't do it. She'd come out the farm, and so mothered this other lady, and she wasn't really a dressmaker, but she had good taste, and she dressed well, and she'd make my dress. And I remember I had a rose, kind of a dusty rose wool, and it had silk in it, but it looked like real fine wool. And they had some kind of braid on it or something like that, but it was real. It was as nice as anybody would wear, you know. And then I always got a coat when I needed it, but I wouldn't maybe wear my coat two or three winters. And then summer dresses, I'd have at least two or three good ones, you know, that I could wear.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you always dressed up when you went to work?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mother usually made my dresses.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Except for the very special ones.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, that was when she had before, you know, before when she had. But later, like when I went to high school, mother made my high school dress for my graduation, and I say that I can remember that it was the prettiest one of all. But we didn't have a big high school class, because most of the girls, or most of the boys too, my brother included, one of the oldest brothers, they went to the prep of the university, and that was high school. See, they had to have a prep at the high school. I think it was 1913 or 15, I don't remember. 1913, I rather think, that they did away with that. No, it was 13, it wasn't later, that they didn't have a prep. Because, see, by that time, the high schools in the state had become accredited high schools, and they didn't need that prep. And then the high school here became a bigger high school. But when I graduated from high school, there were only six girls and one boy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, so the boys mostly had gone to work someplace else.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't know why that. No, I think more the boys went to the prep, like my brother did.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But the girls, you know how girls are, they like to have their school friends, and most of the girls went to high school. And, of course, when I went to college, which was later, I graduated from high school in 1909. And when I graduated from high school, I had already gone up to university. And because I got through high school, I had to have a certain number of credit stands or university fees. And I got my credit for high school work finished, mostly in the third or the first semester of the last year. And so I went to college and took 12 credits. And the principal of the high school talked me into that. I was a bashful country girl, and I was. But I hadn't heard of a woman.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was the principal a man or a woman?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: A man.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Why do you think he saw you as special ability?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he just thought that you hadn't got very much to do the rest of the year. He said, if you want to take some work up to university, you can. All right, I had lots of determination, and I got that from both my mother and father. We just really had. There were a lot of farmers that didn't do near as well, but we just stuck to it. Just like I'm stuck to my legs here. I've got bad legs. But I just sat here, because that's what I'm supposed to do. And I sat here. I don't sit, though, because I have dinner with good people in for dinner, and I have one or two. I do a lot. I keep busy all the time. God gave me two hands, and I use them. I used to tell the waitresses that. I said, oh, get to work. I said, you know, we've got a lot of work to do. Get going. And I said, you know, God gave you two hands, and use them. They remembered that. One thing they remembered, they just told me about that later, and that's the way I grew up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it was kind of, not very many women went to college in those days.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, that's right. I was, and the principal, well, I liked people. The teachers like me, I never crossed them. I never had any trouble with the teachers. And they liked me, and they thought that I was ambitious. And I think that high school people or teachers can be a big, a good influence, or any teacher for that matter, or anybody, can be a good influence if they really like the children and put their effort in to try to say a good word.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They take a real interest in the students. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You've got to, you can't be selfish in this world. You've got to do something for others. In fact, when I catch myself thinking sometimes, I think, well, after all, I believe I think of others most of the time. I don't, and my brothers and nephews said, well, think about yourself. And that's what they told me at the hotel. Think about yourself once in a while. You ought to think about what you should do for this and that one. And I'd be so tired sometimes, but, oh, I guess I got cranky sometimes. But then I had a great income because I just worked terribly hard.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, that kind of, most women got married at the time when you were going to school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know, but I don't think they did. I think that went farther back, you know. See, now like my mother, see, my father was born in the old country, in that island, in the old, it's an island in the Baltic Sea.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, you told me all about that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and then he came over here, and he came to Philadelphia. Then into Chicago, then to Colorado, and he worked in the mines in Colorado. And I told him the book about how he said goodbye to his mother, and I think I told you that maybe. And then he came to, he and his brother and two other men, left the mines together. His brother was older than he was, and he had come later. He didn't come, my father came first. And they were going to take up a homestead. They'd heard about the homestead in Washington, the state of Washington. Well, when they got there, it was out in Pasco, and there wasn't anything but a desert, desert, desert, desert. And they took up this homestead, got this land. They thought, well, there's a river, Columbia River's right near, and they'll surely have water there. But then they did have, too, you know, but then that's a long time later. And so my father and his brother and the other two men, they said, well, we can never make it here. And they had bought plows and some farm equipment, and they went to, they heard about the railroads coming in up near Spokane Falls, they called it, Spokane Falls. And it's before there was a city of Spokane. And, of course, Spokane Falls was really Spokane, a free runner of Spokane. And so they went there, and my father, I'll always remember that he, they had become acquainted with an Indian woman. They used to haul, take them across the river once in a while. I don't know why. She'd cart people across the river.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where was this, in Spokane?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was up in Pasco.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Pasco, across the Columbia.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, but it wasn't right at Pasco, but it was near there. And he showed us, they called it Horse Heaven. And it's a little locality around there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This Indian woman ran kind of a ferry.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, she didn't have a real ferry, but she'd just take them on horseback. Oh. And they had horses. And they had some horses, Indian coyotes, as they called them, and were going to farm. But they left their boots and their, buried their boots in their machinery, he said, and head for Spokane Falls.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So nobody would steal them. Yeah, well. They're most valuable.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't suppose they ever went back there for it. I never did learn that. And then my father got this contract, and I think I told you about that. I've got that in a book. So if you, do you have a book?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, yes, I have a book.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you read that about the Redwood days, because that's the beginning of the Northern Pacific. Oh, I'm glad you have it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And Anne's read it, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And so you can have some of those things. Now, like the high school kids, I have quite a few of them come here. Because I can't un-cum my licks. I can't go up there and up those steps. And Stan Smith has been real nice, and I've just had some real nice kids. I'm all for these young people. I think they're going to save this country, I sure say this. And we hear a lot about the bad ones, but we hear about the bad people. And the whole trouble is the cities are just overcrowded. They just, all the blacks and everybody's gone to cities. Well, if they done like they did in the olden days, got their land and farmed it, but now it's too expensive. But there's a way of doing that. Now, they could have some equipment that the county would buy, or some arrangement like that, to help these smaller farms. And look at all the land here. If you'd been in Europe, you'd realize how much more land we have than they have there, and what they've done with their land there in the Scandinavian countries, in Holland. If they've got a patch of land as big as this room, they've got their racing bulbs.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They make more use of their land than they do here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They don't waste even a square foot. Right. And their streets were narrow, you know, up to now. They still can't do much about their narrow streets. They have to use them. But they have small cars. They don't have big cars. Not very many. Some of them have big cars. And some of the highways are wider and better. Like in Paris, we went from Paris down to Fontainebleau, and that was 25 miles. But packed. Oh, it was tourist material. They were so packed and traffic was so bad that we didn't get to see the things that we were supposed to see that day. We were way behind schedule.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, tell me about most women when you were in college.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When I went to college, there were quite a few. There weren't very many Moscow people, but there were quite a few girls in college. In fact, I think the average maybe was almost as much as, I don't suppose it was ever 50%.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it was more nearly 50% than it is today.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah. But there were.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think made the difference? There were proportionately more women in college then.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Than now? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You think so?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'll tell you. I think that maybe the average girl, I have one little high school girl that's married. I had a student here, and he had graduated from the Idaho. He was president of the farmhouse, and I had him here from September until Christmas. Then he got married, and when he got through here, and he's 28 years old, going 29 I think now, and he went to, he taught up at Worley. That's a small school in Colts there, and taught in the high school there, in a small high school. Worley's up there by Courtney. I know where it is. And this girl went to school there, and she was 17. Well, they got married, and she wasn't going to go to college. No, she didn't want to go to college. I said, listen here, Paul, you just talk her into it, or else let me talk her into it. We're just going to see if that girl wants to go to college. At least try it. If she doesn't, you're going to be, here you're taking your master's degree, a new graduate, once you've got a degree, and he's taking a master's degree, getting his master's in PE, and then when you get through here, you're going to be a coach. That's what you want to be, and you're going to get a job, all right? And here, little Kay, she thinks she's happy now she's in the law, and you're worse, I said. And I said, you just haven't even given it a thought, have you? And he thought I was quite an inspiration, because I talked about him saving. I said, you kids, I said, you've got to learn, you young people have to learn to save. You're just plain throwing time and money away, time and money. I said, I mean time and money. You don't spend ten times as much money, you use it all.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you think it's just as important for a woman to get an education as a man.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, but I don't think it's absolutely necessary to go to college, all of them. I don't think some of the, either boys or girls, need to go to college if they're not going to be, if they don't want to go to college, they may be, it's because they don't know what college can do for them. But they ought to have some kind of a goal, and if they can't go to college to see their way to go to college, and nowadays it's so expensive, that's all right. But I said, what college did for me, maybe it won't do for everybody. And I was a bashful country girl if I ever was one. My mother didn't get farther than through the sixth or seventh grade, sixth I believe, and my father didn't, had all his education in the old country. And both of them were smart, and my goodness, my mother could read and read and was up and coming all the time. They traveled some later when they could, and she was alert, and she learned all she could. She could sit, I can remember my mother sitting there on the farm, turning that old big old churn around, making butter, and she had a baby in her arm. And then she was going to read those magazines. She had serials in the magazine that she wanted to read, and she had the magazine in her other arm, and held it in this arm where the baby was, because she was churning with the other one. And I can remember that. Well, she got all of it done. She got the butter made, and she prepared the baby, and she got her churning done.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What were the names of some of the magazines she took?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, Ladies Home Journal, and I see, oh, Reader's Guide, this was at home. My dad used to read that. And I see there was another news magazine. And mothers read books. Oh, my mother...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you get from the library? Did they have libraries then?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Carnegie Library?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Church library.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Church library.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they had little church libraries. One mother came from Minnesota, see, and she was 13 years old when she came here, and she told me that when she came... In fact, she was born in Sweden, but she was only about four or five years old when she came here with her parents. And my father was born on this island, but my mother was born on the west side, near Gothenburg, and Jönköping, Jönköping. I've learned Swedish, so I can say it. And I've done that since I came here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How old were you when you started learning Swedish?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How old were you? Well, I suppose I heard some at home, because after all, they... But my mother and father didn't talk, scarcely ever talking at home. But my grandfather and grandmother, they didn't understand English very well, so mother could talk to them. And mother said she had the Bible and the catechism, they called it, see, the catechism, and a Bible history. That was all that she'd ever read before she came to America. When she came to Minnesota, why, they didn't have a Swedish church where they lived. My grandfather got a job with the railroad, and my grandmother, she cooked sometimes in a boarding house. But she just had this girl, you know, a little girl. And they had, she had nice clothes, because she had aunts and that, that gave her clothes. And grandpa and grandma had just one, and they were making money, good enough, not what you call a lot of money, but making money so that they could keep, have a nice home, and a fairly nice home, a plain home. But they had nice furniture here. They had four or five homes here, and grandfather was a landscaping gardener. He'd learn it by himself. And he went, and mother went to the Presbyterian Church, and they had a library there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did the women establish the library? Well, the congregation. How did they, the garden, just the congregation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, the congregation. And then she said that her Sunday school teacher, well, she loved her Sunday school teacher. Her name was Mrs. Preston. She went back about 35 years afterwards. She had surgery back then. She wanted to go back there at the Mayo Clinic. And she went back there, and she went to see her, and she found her. She was there, that Sunday school teacher. She remembered her. And it was so sweet to hear.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She was an inspiration to her, her Sunday school teacher was.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, but she said, you keep things so nice and clean, and you look so nice and clean all the time. She said, I'm going to let you take a book home to read whenever you want it. You'll be sure and bring it back. And mother said yes. She said, I just read everything they had in that library. And then other kids have books at home, and they found out she liked them. So my mother read books a lot. Even to her dying day, she was 78. And she died in 51, right here in Moscow. Her home's in the, her last home's in the book there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And do you think, she had 10 children. Now this is kind of a personal question. Do you think she really wanted 10 children?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, I think she did. She said that when she was alone, she had loaned so much. She said, when I get married, I'm going to have nine children. I don't know why she said nine, but she did. She always said she said that when she grew up. She's going to have nine children.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she got what she wanted plus ten.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And all of them lived to maturity. My oldest brother died in 54, and my brother died three years ago here. He stayed here with me, with the widows. He had married twice, and both of them had died of cancer. Well, one of them didn't die of cancer. She died of encephalitis. She didn't know him for three weeks, a month. Well, but you asked me about the college, girls going to college. And I think that I gave you that example of this one girl that was just crazy to get married. Well, they come up to see me real often. I had them for dinner one night this week. I'm trying to be nice to them, but I told her, I said, or I told him first. And I told her, too. I said, you're going to get a job, and she isn't going to know a thing about college, and be interested in it. You're going to cease to be so interested in her. You're not going to have any problems. And I said, you just can't expect to be real happy or have much in common if you're that far apart. If you're training, it's that far apart. And I said, you better just talk her into going. I said, if she only goes one year, do like I did to my sister, my little sister. She was my little sister always. And she's Mrs. George Klein now, the boy's the youngest. And her husband had charge of Censor Church's office. Censor Church could even be a president someday, you never can tell. And he's doing a real good job. And George came from California and came up here to go to Idaho and take forestry. And he ended up by taking agriculture. And he had never even seen a cow hardly before. Didn't know what, oh, they just kidded him on the farm because he said he was going to make a table for the calf. A table for the calf. He made a little stall for the calf and a place to feed that calf. And he called it the table for the calf. And the boys out on the farm, of course, they got the biggest kick out of that to make a table for the calf. But George hadn't hardly seen a cow in Oakland, California. His father was German and he came from Germany and he became a construction man and a very wealthy man. And the mother was raised where Chinatown is now. That was her father's farm. But she was of German descent too. But she came up here and he said, after I came to Idaho I didn't ever want to go back to California. And his folks couldn't understand it. They said, why did he want to go to Idaho, to that university, when he could go to Berkeley right there at our back door? Well, George wanted to go to Idaho. And George loved it in Idaho. George loves Idaho. They're both loyal alums of this university. Their son is too. That's the father of those three children. And then they had another boy. I've got to tell you this story about George coming to college and meeting my sister there. And she wasn't going to take home ec, because Elsie took home ec. And see, I really got my degree in biology because I took all this work in high school before I started college, or in college, before I finished high school. And so I had to kind of take what they thought that I had taken botany in high school and liked it and got good grades in it. And why didn't I take botany? All right, there's a nice old fellow by the name of Aldrich, Professor Aldrich. He was my main instructor in botany all the way through college. And he was really a smart man. He got a real nice job in Washington, DC later. And so I took botany. But I took 21 credits a semester every year after I got there. And I got through in 3 and 1⁄2 years. And then I went back one year afterwards. And I didn't get a school that year. Schools weren't very plentiful. So I went back one year and thought I'd get my home X. But my mother got sick, and that's when she went back to Mayo Brothers. Back to Mayo Brothers, to that place where I told you she lived in Waseda, Minnesota, where the Mayo Clinic is. And I just lacked about three weeks of finishing, three or four weeks of finishing. And I was going to go back and take it, but I got a school that year. And I taught school for three years. And you might say country school. And Winchester was a nice little town. But I just didn't really like teaching there. I liked it. I liked the subject matter real well. And this was hard for me because I liked to teach too well. And so when I came home here, I came home here in the summer. And I decided then that Mr. Wright wanted me to come there to the hotel, and I'd finish. And I'd take more home X than most any of all the graduates, except that I did lack some chemistry. But they required a lot more chemistry than they do now. And so I just said, well, I'd take that job at the hotel. And I told him I'd be there one year. I promised him. Instead of one year, I stayed 37 years, 36 years, counting that one year off for my trip. And so that's the way that worked out. Why did you never marry? I don't know how many people have told me. I just thought. My sisters, my brothers, I guess, had the best of wishes. They said, well, if anybody treats Elsie any different than her seven brothers, she doesn't want to have anything to do with mine. I said, I can love a man just as much as anybody.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just never did find the right man to marry, or you just didn't want to get married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I just got so involved. I think that's the only reason. I just got so involved in my work there and knew so many people. And I thought, well, there were lots of people that wanted to take me for a ride, take me on a date, and wanted to do this and wanted to do that. And I always did when I got to be by myself. I thought, well, if I give up being with these people, being just the wife of one man, I don't know whether I'll like it or not. And I like all the men.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just had to give up too much to marry one man.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's just right. And they just treated me so nice. And that's what the brothers did. They just all treated her like brothers. And she loved it. And he said, why did my, I called him Whitey, he had the name Oscar. He said, why was I named after the king of Sweden? I said, now listen, you know, I found something out when I went to Sweden. I found out that the first king of Sweden was Bernadotte, and he was French. She wasn't a Swede at all. Well, but, now where did we leave off? There were some things that, oh, I want to just finish telling you about George Clyde, how he came to Idaho and never went back. And then he went off to the farm. And the farm, of course, was just home to us. And I mean home, and we loved it, all of us. We were a close family, and we loved it. I don't mean to say we didn't have any, some of them, like this brother, he was ornery. We all, any family, you know that. I don't know how many children you have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I have three.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, but anyhow, that's a nice family. And I always used to say, well, Mother, I'm not going to get married until I'm, what was it, 29, 39? 39, I think I used to tell her. I'm not going to get married until I'm 39, because I don't want to have as many children as you have.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You said that at home. You observed her having to work pretty hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, it was hard.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What would she answer to that? What would she answer?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: She said, well, maybe you'll be like me. She said that when you find somebody you like real well, while you're marrying them, you don't care whether you're 29 or 19 or 15. But they wouldn't let her get married at 15. She was 13 when she came to this town, and she got married when she was 17, a little better than 17.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And it was pretty young, wasn't it? That's right. And she picked striding and went to work.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And my father was 12 years older than she, but that was common in those days. And that's what I say, that there were very few girls. All these real mothers came in here, and these men took up homesteads, and some of them weren't married. And there were a lot of men, young men here. And there was a lot of work. You know, the university was built, and a lot of work. And there weren't very many girls to pick from. And so when my mother had, she had dozens of suitors, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She had her choice, then, didn't she?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, she really did. And that's the way that was. But I guess it was meant to be that way. But she did a good job, and they were congenial. I can remember when we used to have Connie Farris at Spokane every year. Real nice ones, too. I didn't get to go, but Mother and Dad went to one. And the Davenport was new, the Davenport Restaurant, not the hotel. The Davenport Restaurant. And my mother had not had her honeymoon yet. And there were five children, I think, six. And this Fred, I remember I had to take care of him, and he was fifth one. I had to start from the top and the bottom. And then I took care of them for several days, and they went up to the fair in Spokane. And Dad, they did pretty good on the farm. And then my father did excavating. He helped with road work and different things at odd times. He'd have cattle, and they'd sell to him or some cattle or something like that for extra money. And so that's where we got along better. And we just had 240 acres from that home farm. And believe me, we never were hungry or never were cold either. We had wool blankets, and we slept in an unheated upstairs. There was one stove upstairs in Mother's room, and she'd let us come in there and dress when it's real cold. But I got up at 5 o'clock and walked to school when it was dark. And I walked to that railroad crossing and walked down that railroad, and it was dark. And when I came home, I had math classes until 5. I had home ec lab classes in chemistry and biology. I had lots of math classes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When your sisters were growing up, you helped them some, didn't you? Didn't you have a tea room down in the little school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I had a tea room. My little sister stayed there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You sent them to school down there?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The reason she stayed with me, though, was mainly because she walked from the farm, and that was hard for her. And the other boys were nearly all grown up, and they didn't want to be bothered by their little sister. So when I was there, she stayed there, and I loved to have her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, what are some of the differences you see with the way children grew up when you grew up, and what your grandnieces and nephews are?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, no, I don't think there's much difference. If they're the kind that are taught well, like my nephew, this nephew, he's doing real well, and they've got their home. And George and Elvira are their parents, and they've got this, well, they just had Doug, and then they had this brother, or son, who got his doctorate in chemistry, and he got an MSS, if it matched, Foundation of Science scholarship for $29, $100 a year for four years, or until he got through. And he went back to Minnesota, because he could go to Northwestern or St. Paul, not St. Paul, the universities in Minneapolis, I think, or Washington. But he went there because it's the best chemistry school. And when he finished, he was all through, but his advisor wanted to work with him for several weeks before he left. And so when he had his paper all done, I don't think he had to write a thesis. He'd done a lot of research for him. I don't believe he had to write a thesis, but he was going to get his doctor's degree in chemistry. And another boy who'd gone to school up, who had been a classmate of his and had attended Washington University, he came there and stopped to see him. And he was going to Washington, D.C. for some advanced information, something that he needed in his work. I don't know what that was. And this Bill had met a girl. He met her in Minneapolis, but I don't know how he happened to meet her. She was from Iowa, and she went to school, but not where he did. Because there were several students of his classmates that had apartments, had two apartments, and then they kind of lived in two apartments, but they cooked and danced. And so he announced his engagement to this girl, and her mother was there from Iowa. And they were having a party for him. And this advisor was going to be there, and some of the other faculty people. They thought a lot of him. He had a good point. He was really a nice kid. Oh, he was a real nice boy. And he'd had different girls, but he had got this girl, and they announced their engagement in the afternoon. And that evening, they were going to have their party for him. He was going down to get some snacks. They wanted something for their little feed that they were going to have. And the girl didn't want to go because she was tired. And he'd given her the ring and everything. So she told him, well, why don't you have this bill or whatever his name was, go with you instead, and take my car because it's outside here. And so they did. And, you know, both of them were killed instantly, just instantly. A fellow didn't stop, you know, and he was sort of drunk and so on. His father had been in jail, and I don't know what all. And he just draped their bodies on the ground. It's the saddest thing, but then we just have to forget it. His father just never can get us to forget. But then they had this girl. She's 10 years younger than Bill, Mary Ann. And she graduated from college in Portland. And last year, two years ago maybe, yes, two years, and she's been teaching. And now I talk to my sister. She talks to me real often from Boise. And she said, well, Mary Ann announced her engagement. She'll be 24 this August, so we're real happy about it. Both her mother and father. She's done well, too. Well, they're not – I wouldn't say that our family has any brilliant people. Maybe some of them are, though. They're solid citizens. Good, solid citizens. Good, solid citizens. Now, this oldest brother, he's 80. He was 80 the other day. And he lives in California. And he built a new home up at Tess Darrow. That's where his daughter lives. He has two sons and one daughter. And they built this nice home. And the one son has his home overlooking the Pacific up at Palace Reserves. That's the exclusive district in Los Angeles. And he has a very good job with sort of a refrigeration system. And he has, I think, 11 states. It seems to me like it's 11 states that he looks after. When I say looks after, I don't know what other word to use. But he has some supervision of those 11 states for that company. And he's gone one week, and then he's home one week. And he really has his office at home. But he's making real good money, and they live in a beautiful home. They bought one home and fixed it up. I was there. I've been in California many times. And I was there, and then they had just moved, and they traded that old home in on a nicer one. But it was some doctor and his wife separated. She couldn't keep the home and take care of it because it didn't have that income after she was separated. And so he got it, and they paid for that. And it's just really beautiful.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, it seems like a farm's a pretty good place to raise a family.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, you're right. I just think about that. Our farm is ideal because it's only two miles away from town.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So you had some advantages being near the university too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and the university and everything. All of them didn't graduate from the university, but at the same time, they just really absorbed a lot of it. Those boys that walked, the older ones and the younger ones, walked to town for all the basketball games and football games. They didn't miss any of them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was your recreation in those days.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and well, it still is, I guess.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, true.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And of course, their, and this one brother, he got a job with the Air Force, Department of Commerce, Bureau of Aeronautics, and he retired from the government. You know, they retire early. He's only in his 50s when he retired. And then he lives in Phoenix. And they were up here last summer. And he gets a real, well, I think he gets $600 or $700. Well, with the Airwest, when he got through there, he got a job with the Airwest, and he's kind of a consultant. But he's retired now entirely. But he gets something like, oh, I imagine he gets $600 or $700 a month retirement. Now, you asked me some questions.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I guess one thing, you've already answered a lot of them, but I remember you're talking about how you had pretty much, after your father died and your mother lived in Moscow, you had quite a bit of responsibility for taking care of her when she was older, didn't you? No. No, the whole family did it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, no. I didn't have to because, for one thing, my mother was like me. She was 78 years old when she died, and of course, that's younger than I am. But she was really only sick, very sick, for seven months. And she had the means to take care of her. And what baffled me was that we found out, I did, because I was at the hotel and she had her home up here. And she lived up there, and she had this kind of a slight stroke. She had hardening in the arteries, and she had terrible headaches. So she was sick that way, but maybe she'd been that way for seven or eight years that it bothered her. But she just defied the thought of getting down or not enjoying life and traveling. She loved to travel, and she felt so bad sick that she and Dad couldn't travel together. And they never did get to it except just short trips, you might say. And then the last question she had, we just had nurses around the clock. And we didn't ask any of us to do anything about the finances because she had the credit to take care of that. We thought it was so wonderful to think that after Dad died, well, let's see how long did she live. He died on the 32nd, and she died on the 51st.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she lived almost 20 years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and she managed the farm and that. And with my brother, she ran it to my brother, but she kept the farm until she died.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So she made decisions clear up to the very end.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, and was able to until I say the seventh month or so. And she was bright as could be, and she worried about me working so hard and never taking any time off to rest or anything. But I did go to California several times on short trips. One time the Kiwanis gave me a ticket, a flight, bought a flight for me to go down. She was down there. And I had a hernia operation. Yeah, and I really got it. I had a heavy old typewriter, and I just lifted that typewriter, lifted it up, and I just felt it. And I had a hernia operation. But it didn't affect my health, really. My blood and everything like that was perfect. It was just my legs, and I just wore them out at the hotel because I had bad veins, otherwise I wouldn't have made it. And so my mother had a checking account of $8,000, and that was quite a bit, you know. Even in 51, that was a big checking account. And then she had the farm, and she had the building that my father bought that building down on where the university pharmacy, not the university pharmacy, but the florist.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Moscow Florist.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, well, I still, and I bought that, see. But I sold it because I didn't want to be bothered about remodeling and all this and that. But I said I didn't want the money, so I just kept the name. And I still have five or six years to go. So I don't have to worry about nothing. And then my brother left some of his estate, because his wife was gone and he didn't have any children except his doctor. He had one boy that was his first wife's son, and he's a neurosurgeon, so he can take care of his family.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: This group of women that we're working with, we're interested in getting people to appreciate what women have contributed to Idaho. Not only men, but women aren't written up that much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I know it. Well, I'm not for all this new, you know, what do you call it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The women's movement?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'm for the women's movement. I'm all for that. But all these women that are trying to get in and taking men's jobs and all that, I don't approve that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What do you think about that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't. I don't think so. I think that it's all right if they're capable, really smart women. And I know a lot of smart women. There are a lot of smart women in this world, and a lot of the husbands and that don't give their wives credit for some of it, and they could do better than they do. I know that. I've worked with men and women the best part of my life, and I've been told a lot of things that I never tell, but both men and women, and I always made it a point. If he tells me or she tells me, don't tell them. That's the way.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But you're saying it's in the...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I'm not for this, what do you call it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Women's liberation?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm just all for that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You think that some of the women aren't qualified?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think that, but I think that our economy, not our economy, but our social life will be at stake because I think it's going to mess things up too much. And a lot of women that have become... I listen to TV a lot because I've got time now, and I get up in the morning early, I look at that 7 to 9 program. The Today Show? Yeah, and there's some good talkers on that. And I always listen to the Washington Week in Review, and I always listen to Wall Street. I don't buy stocks and bonds because I don't know enough about it, for one thing. But if I did, why, I'd just stick my money in the bank and get, if I get 7 and 1 quarter for a lot of it, why, that's a good place to keep it. When you get my age, you might just as well do that. And I just think, now I could get Social Security, and I wouldn't live that well on Social Security.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I see now.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I've paid for this home since I've been here. I still owe a little bit on it because my brother-in-law, this George, he's a real smart man, and he says, Elsie, you sure are using your head when you don't pay for that house because you only pay 6% and you get 7 and 1 quarter. Why, that's good business not to pay for your house. He said, don't worry about this house. They're taking care of it. I don't even bother about it. They just take it out of my account every month. Out of my escrow, I pay for the house, and I haven't got much left.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But what you're saying about the women's liberation is that women should stay at home more?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I wouldn't say that all. There's no definite answer for that because a lot of women, the ones that want to get out, a lot of women, you're just a mother and all that, but a lot of women, they just love the idea of getting away from their family. Some of the sad things that I know and I've heard about the families that are really neglected is because the women get so involved in their jobs. I have a lot of people come here, not only that, not here, but I've been in public life, and I just know that that's true, and I don't blame them. But now, like my mother, she couldn't do it because she had too many, but if my mother had had time and gone out and got a job, my father wouldn't have objected to it, and she wouldn't have neglected her home or her family, but she would have maybe done her job and taken care of her home. And so I don't see how there couldn't be an answer to that. But like Barbara Walters, you know, on that program, she has different people on there that she talks to, and they've had a lot of these women, and some of these women are smart. You know that. There are women in this United States that could make a good person or a better person than some of the ones we have, and I'm sure a lot of them that would... I think about Governor Samuelson. I don't know what... Governor Samuelson. Well, I... Say, are we going to have a little bit of tea or something?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, we're just taking so much of your time. I'm just about finished here. You must be getting thirsty, though.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I'm not worried about you or your... but what about your kids?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, my husband's home with them.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, all right. Well, I just wanted to ask you,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: before we finish recording here, I wanted to tell you that we're making a presentation, and we have a program, and one portion of the program is about Elsie Nelson, and Anne Goodwin does the reading. And I wanted to know if she... She came to meet you and everything, and I wanted to know if she had any questions to ask you now that I haven't. She's read the book.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Why don't you tell me something about this lady? What...about your life? Now, I've been looking at you, and I've been saying, if you sat over there, maybe I could have looked at you.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: She's been listening to you.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I don't... I told the history prof, I just don't talk very well. I don't ever...never... I hated to recite when I was a kid, and even in college. And I remember one of my English teachers said, Elsie, she said, you can recite. You just don't...you just think you can't. You just make up your mind to do it. And, you know, I tried to get...think about that. But now, like, I can write. I just...I just write. I just love to write just by the yard. And I'm going to write... I'm going to write a lot of things that they didn't let me put in my book, see. Because it would have made the book too... too complicated and too much family, so that it wouldn't have been made this saleable.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, you certainly should get that written down.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And so I'm going to do that. And I...this nephew, I told you, he has a credit bureau. And he's got a...he has extra time, and he's ambitious like I am. I guess the whole Nelson family was, really. And he...or maybe it was Klein family, the German part of them. And he got a printing press, and he does a real good job. See, I've made...I've already made a little... besides my book, I've got a little... what is it you call it? All the birthdates and the generations.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Genealogy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've got that separate, see. Because I couldn't put it in the book. So I got all the information I could. I didn't go back to the church. I went back there. I was in that church, but then that... that would have taken too long to get. And even if I'd gotten that information, gotten those names and that, I wouldn't have gained very much. Because one of my cousins, he's the second or third cousin, is a minister. And he went back there, and he had them open that chest and get that information. But he copied it, or took pictures of it. And he can't read those names. They're written in the old script most of them. And he can't...I could read it. Because I learned that German script, and that's the old script, you know. And I've had a lot of Germans in French. But so I thought, well, I surely can learn Swedish. And I've had a lot of fun with my Swedish, because those cousins in Stockholm, one cousin, she's three years older than I am. And she...three or four. And she had studied English, you know, and went to school in Paris. But then she had been away from it for so long, and she'd rather read the Swedish, see. So I said, all right, I'll read it. But I'll write it. But whether you can read it or not, I don't know. And she said, I think you do fantastically well, she said. So we...and I said, you write Swedish, and I'm going to answer you in Swedish. And so I write. But then her letters sound a lot better to me than mine do. To her, I'm sure. But she really... They just love you. And I think it was worth an awful lot to get to go there and find that real genuine hospitality, not only hospitality, but genuine family adoration and love that they showed me. And they're that way. And I was so happy when I went to Spokane. I went about twice a year to have my feet taken care of, my toes and corns and cows, which I used to have a lot of them, but I don't have too many anymore. But even then, I don't dare even trim my toenails because my family said, no. All right, I'll obey. I'll go up to Spokane. That gives me a good day off. And I still can go. I'm going pretty soon, again. But maybe my brother will take me up in the car. But if he doesn't, I'll go on the bus. And that's the way my mother went. And... Don't we... I'd gone to him about 20 years my mother went to. She used to go about every month. She'd go up on the bus and back until her dying day, just about. And so this doctor said, didn't you tell me that you were writing a book one time? I hadn't been there for quite a long time. I think I skipped it. I went to Boise and I had my feet taken care of there, so I skipped a few months. And he said, yes. He said, you said that you went to the... Your father was born on an island in the Baltic Sea. I said, that's right. He said, do you know where he went there? He said, just like that. He didn't talk very much, this doctor, but he's a nice man. And he said, we went there last summer. It was this last... Not now, not this summer, but last year. And his name is McAlpine. I said, what were you doing in the Baltic Sea?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was a name like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, a name like that. And so he said, well, I had more fun than I ever had in my life, and I just didn't want to go again so bad that I think we'll go again. All right? Now, that means the we part of it, we means your wife. And he said, yes, I married one of them. All right, I said, you did make a good choice. And she's delightful. I had to meet her right now. So the next time I went, he had told me this. So then I called up for an appointment, and I said, this time I'm going to meet Mrs. McAlpine. And he had given me his address because I asked for it. And I wrote to her, and I told her I'm coming up there, and I'm going to meet you. I said, that's just one more friend I'll have, one more good friend. I know it'll be a good friend. And that's two years now since, just about, not quite. And so we arranged, and she told me to come up to her house. I said, no, it's no use trying to do that. They live far out, and I wouldn't do that. But they arranged for a meet. We were going to meet at the Crescent, have lunch at the Crescent. My brother, my one brother lives here, and his wife, and they took me up. So we all had lunch. But we talked, and we sure had a good time. And so that's, and I just love to meet those people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You do like to meet new people, don't you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I just love people. Because I just like people.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was wondering if maybe we're giving this presentation here in Moscow next Friday night. And I think it, wouldn't it be fun? Wouldn't you like to come and see it? Could I come and get you?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I might be embarrassed, huh?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think you're the only.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm not going to be embarrassed for you really. I'm not going to be embarrassed.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, probably I'd be able to resist saying that Elsie Nelson is in the audience. But it'd be hard if you wanted me to. I'd resist. But it'd be nice to be able to say we have Elsie Nelson in the audience.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I suppose now.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But there might be people there who know you. I'm sure there would be.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I don't care about that anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But I would like to come and get you if you'd like to come.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think that's real nice of you, and I suppose there's no reason why I couldn't go. I might not be. I haven't got any new clothes lately, but then.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You have a beautiful dress on right now. I've been admiring it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is my standby, and I've had it two years now, and I wash it, see. My sister washed it when I was in Boise. I don't like to wash it very well. I mean, she does a better job. She's a better housekeeper. We're going to have some tea, though.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you have time? Cookies.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If you haven't got time. What time is it? Well, listen, if you don't have time. Now, you tell me about yourself. Am I as interested in you as somebody else? I'm more interested in finding out a bit more about your years at the Moscow Hotel during the Great Depression. All right, that's easy.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's easy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I read how you. . . It's one sentence that I want to. . . Hotel. No, it's in the front. I think I marked it. Put that in there. I wish we could find it right away quick. Well, let's see. I. . . I hadn't planned to write my book yet when I retired, but I did have it in the back of my mind that I wanted to leave a message for my brothers and sisters. And I would try to write a bibliography or my story of our family, a typical family of the pioneer days. And it's written up in the book. You try to find that and read it. And I don't. . . just find it right away. I could even call you, tell you after you leave. But the most interesting part of my life at the hotel was meeting all these people, learning to know them. And they became very dear friends. When Ted Pritchard died, two of those, my old Coleman friends who used to eat there all the time, called me up. And one of them came over here to see me. And I thought that was real nice because they knew that he meant a lot to me because he had designed my home. And I had . . . as director of foods, I had complete charge of the food service in the hotel. And that meant not the daily meal planning, but entirely alone with the chef I did, because he knew more about the meat. And I bought the meat and he planned the meat. But I always would make suggestions about the meal and the rest of the meal I usually planned. And my idea coincided with my boss, Mr. Wright. He thought that everybody should be satisfied. And he didn't care whether I sold . . . And he planned that I should figure to serve the food at a cost that was within the reach of the average person so that nobody felt disappointed when they left. That was his theory and that's mine. And we agreed perfectly on that. He said, if I don't make any money on the dining room, I'll come out on it by having a good dining room. And I want you to make it the best you know how. So I grew up on the job and my home-made background was a help. But then I had a lot to discover and a lot to learn. And I had learned . . . my mother was a good organizer and I tried to be. So I feel like that's one reason that I was successful. And our food business grew from a very small amount to a large amount. In fact, I shouldn't quote prices, I guess, but we had as much as $100,000 to business a month. Some good months. That's a lot of food to plan and care for.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Naturally is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And have somebody serve it. And we always . . . I was allowed to have all the help I needed. Have as many waitresses as I needed, busboys or anything, all the help I needed. And Mr. Wright said, I know you won't go overboard on that because you're conservative. And he said that's the way we want it. And don't try to do too much yourself. Just tell the rest of them to do it. And I said that wasn't very satisfactory because, I mean, to try to leave it all to the help. You don't get that kind of help. For example, the first luncheon I served there was for Mrs. David, the mother of David. You know, the David store. How long have you been here?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Three years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, so you didn't know him then. Well, and they had heavy old hotel dishes. That's one of the first things I wanted to do was to change their dish pattern. It was too much like a greasy-jawed restaurant. And I had been at the Blue Bucket and served lunch there, and a lot of people had been there. And that's why the town women knew me, see, and knew what I could do. And they were thrilled when I got this job. And Mr. Wright just begged me, and I said, I'm planning on going to California. And he said, well, just try it anyway for a year. All right. I said I'll stay a year. And they gave me a terrible room. He's dead and gone, so you won't hear. And a terrible, terrible room, but that's all he had, really. That was before they enlarged it. And an old curly two-iron bed and an old, old, old dresser, and a bare floor with one little rug, and a closet big enough to put one or two dresses in, some of my everyday dresses.
