And but our business started to grow, and we served very reasonably. We served dinner for 75 to 85 cents. And Pullman people started to come over, and the Pullman people just made that hotel. One day, on the first Sundays out there, we had two tables of people from Pullman, Pullman faculty people and families. And I went and talked to them, you know, because I knew they weren't Moscow people. I knew most of Moscow people at that time. And they said they were from Pullman. And they were very glad, and they gave me very much encouragement. And within three months, we had this diner, our dining room, filled on Sundays, and maybe two-thirds of them were Pullman people. And so, and then they started to plan their lunches and parties, and it grew so that I had from one social function to three or four, including maybe a banquet or a service group in one day. Many, many days I had that many. And I had to plan those menus. I planned all the special menus. And I had an awful time with the kind of help I had, especially during the war, to get them. I had three menus, one for the girls in the dining room, one for the cooks in the kitchen, and one for the women in the other part of the kitchen, the fancy people. And then I'd be on the job every minute. Those days I didn't even rest 15 minutes from 5 o'clock until maybe 10, 9, and 10. And I took particular care of checking on the girls so that they served the right menu to the right people. And I'd tell them and tell them and tell them. But even once in a while, first thing I know, I said, where are you taking those steaks? In that dining room. I said, take them back right quick. And they were all eating dinner, see. I said, take them back right quick. And I had to get up there to cook. And he had the menu too. And I said, the girls are not serving that dinner yet. They haven't got that dinner. They're taking those steaks to the wrong party. And the sad part of it was that there were steaks at the dinner. And steaks always came off of the grill if I hadn't even do it. That's why my football, serving the football team, was successful. And I want you to read that. That was the most successful thing I did in the hotel was serving the athletes. Because I just got a real good reputation from that. And that's where the football teams would come and the basketball and the baseball and the swimming games and everything. But the basketball and football was the most important. And they came from California and Oregon, Oregon State, Oregon University, Seattle, University of Washington. And we didn't serve the WSU people. But we served Stanford and all those different universities. And they'd just fly in and I'd have the menu. And they'd send the menu lots of times. But the coaches got used to my service. And they said, well, whether we send the menu or not, you know what we feed them. And I knew the coaches personally and knew what their ordinary menus were. And I had to order their meat ahead of time, weeks ahead of time. We ordered in modest bulk. When some of the football teams, we served as many as 50 to 60 steaks. And that took seven or eight loins of beef, choice beef. And I never took a chance on those players being late. Of course, you didn't have to worry much about that because they were like wolves. When Elsie said, come, they were right there. They didn't waste any time. And the coaches were just grand. As soon as the coaches came in, they said, is Elsie around? Well, I was always around. I never missed a time that I wasn't around. I might not have been right there at the dance until they could see me. But I was there. And then they'd say, well, are you all lined up? And after they'd been there a few times, only I had some trouble with an Oregon coach one time. And he grew to be one of my best friends. In fact, I got a letter from the book. Somebody had given him the book, my book. And he wanted to write me a letter. And he's retired now. And all those things are just really gratifying. We couldn't serve 60 steaks on the stove. But I told the coach to tell them or else I'd go in and they'd add them. I had the back room. We had plenty of room for 60 people. And I'd go in there and I'd say, now, some of you are going to wait for the steaks. And they knew that. So we'd put them on and then I'd have the girls and I'd have somebody make the toast. And I'd have somebody dish up the steaks. I'd have somebody get the salsa on. I just had to work like clockwork. And then we'd get them all served. And the boys, they just, well, they would. They just literally, especially the basketball kids, I'd serve them for dinner, see, in the afternoon. We used to serve them, I think, 3 o'clock, somewhere around there. And then at night, after the game, I'd have to have a feed for them. And I had the pantry women make sandwiches. Nearly all, most of them had turkey or chicken sandwiches. And like on Friday, it'd be something different. And the milkshakes, and I'd order them from the fountain, see. And then salad, fruit salad. And I'd have the pantry women make them and put them on trays, big trays, in the big walk-in icebox. And then we'd serve them. And Gregory, L.H. Gregory, he wrote the sports page in the Portland Oregonian. And he'd always come with the teams. And he'd write up the game after the games in the evening, see. And so he wouldn't come when the boys came. They'd shower, and then they'd come down to eat. And Gregory would be late. He and another fellow, usually a trainer or somebody, would be late. And I always waited till he came. And that's what he wrote up in one of them. I've got a whole book, an envelope of clippings that he gave me right up to about three or four different times, see.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He showed me one when I was there the last time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I think that was the one he wrote in the Oregonian now when he found out about my book. And that's Hopson, you know, was the coach. And he was there. Well, I won't take any more time for that. But their daily service was just like any restaurant, I suppose, except that you had to give a little bit more than food. And a lot of them, especially the traveling public and especially the men who were connected with the, oh, we called them salesmen in the old days, you know, the salesmen. And they were there for when we had food salesmen. I had to buy from the garden that I ordered from. I gave them orders. I always tried to give them some orders. But they never talked me into getting something I didn't want. After, they talked to me about twice. Well, that was it. The salesman said, that's what I'm going to have. Well, that's it. I wouldn't take pie fillings and try some new stuff and that that I wouldn't serve because I didn't serve that kind of food. And I said, as long as I'm here, it's going to be fresh food like they used to get at home. It's not going to be pie fillings and jello and nothing but. I said, it's going to be real food. And that's what really helped. And that's something that salesmen especially. And they'd come in. They'd be so tired. Most of them would try to come in a little early. Then there were some of them that tried to make Moscow Hotel at a certain time. And then they'd have their service after.
